course.title: AP U.S. History
course.description: Trace how Americans have argued over identity, power, work, and their place in the world, from the societies that existed before 1491 to the present.
course.previewDescription: Follow the nation's development from early contact and colonization through independence, civil war, industrialization, world wars, and recent decades.

unit.title: Period 3
unit.description: Follow the Seven Years' War, the road to independence, the Revolution, the Articles of Confederation and the Constitution, and the first political parties from 1754 to 1800.

firstTopic.title: Contextualizing Period 3
firstTopic.summary: How the Seven Years' War, British imperial reform, colonial self-government, and Enlightenment ideas set the stage for independence and the first experiments in republican government, 1754–1800.

topic.title: The Articles of Confederation
topic.summary: How the states and the first national government were organized after independence, why the Articles of Confederation proved too weak, and how Congress organized the Northwest Territory.

framework.name: Course themes
framework.title: Use the course themes to choose your evidence
framework.intro: The themes connect developments across all nine periods. A piece of evidence can fit more than one theme; choose the one that answers the prompt.
framework.sourceNote: Theme names, codes, and descriptions follow the AP U.S. History Course and Exam Description (fall 2026).

themes.title: American and National Identity
themes.description: This theme focuses on how and why definitions of American and national identity and values have developed among the diverse and changing population of North America as well as on related topics, such as citizenship, constitutionalism, foreign policy, assimilation, and American exceptionalism.
themes.question: Who counted as American, and what did people believe the nation stood for?
themes.example: Debates over ratifying the Constitution turned on what kind of republic Americans wanted.

themes.title: Work, Exchange, and Technology
themes.description: This theme focuses on the factors behind the development of systems of economic exchange, particularly the role of technology, economic markets, and government.
themes.question: How did people earn a living, trade, and use new technology?
themes.example: Canals and railroads tied farmers in the West to markets in the East.

themes.title: Geography and the Environment
themes.description: This theme focuses on the role of geography and both the natural and human-made environments in the social and political developments in what would become the United States.
themes.question: How did land, climate, and resources shape choices, and how did people change them?
themes.example: The Chesapeake's climate suited tobacco, which shaped its labor system.

themes.title: Migration and Settlement
themes.description: This theme focuses on why and how the various people who moved to and within the United States both adapted to and transformed their new social and physical environments.
themes.question: Why did people move, and how did they change the places they settled?
themes.example: The Great Migration brought African Americans from the rural South to northern cities.

themes.title: Politics and Power
themes.description: This theme focuses on how different social and political groups have influenced society and government in the United States as well as how political beliefs and institutions have changed over time.
themes.question: Who held power, how did they use it, and who challenged it?
themes.example: The New Deal expanded the federal government's role in the economy.

themes.title: America in the World
themes.description: This theme focuses on the interactions between nations that affected North American history in the colonial period and on the influence of the United States on world affairs.
themes.question: How did contact, trade, diplomacy, and war connect America to other nations?
themes.example: The Seven Years' War left Britain in debt and changed its policies toward the colonies.

themes.title: American and Regional Culture
themes.description: This theme focuses on the how and why national, regional, and group cultures developed and changed as well as how culture has shaped government policy and the economy.
themes.question: How did beliefs, religion, arts, and media develop and shape public life?
themes.example: The Second Great Awakening inspired many Americans to join reform movements.

themes.title: Social Structures
themes.description: This theme focuses on how and why systems of social organization develop and change as well as the impact that these systems have on the broader society.
themes.question: How were people ranked by race, class, and gender, and how did that change?
themes.example: The growth of a middle class in the Gilded Age changed ideas about leisure and family.

questions.prompt: Which of the following describes many of the new state constitutions written after 1776?
choices: They gave governors the power to veto laws and to dismiss the legislatures whenever they disagreed
They gave every adult resident the right to vote, regardless of property or sex, and ended all restrictions
They placed the most power in the legislature and kept property requirements for voting and citizenship
They created a single national legislature that governed all of the states through appointed councils
questions.explanation: Americans feared executive power, so most states made the legislature the strongest branch, and many continued to limit voting to property owners.
choiceExplanations: Most states limited the powers of their governors.
Most states kept property qualifications for voting.
Americans feared executive power, so most states made the legislature the strongest branch, and many continued to limit voting to property owners.
State constitutions created state governments.
questions.distinguisher: The universal-suffrage choice is close because the state constitutions spoke of rights, but they kept property qualifications.
questions.subskillText: Identify a historical concept, development, or process.

questions.prompt: Which of the following best explains why most states gave their governors limited powers in the new state constitutions?
choices: British officials required the states to limit their governors as a condition of the Treaty of Paris
Americans feared concentrated executive power after their experience with royal governors and the king
State legislatures had often failed to pass laws, and voters wanted a stronger executive to replace them
The Articles of Confederation ordered the states to give most of their powers to the Congress
questions.explanation: The colonists' experience with the Crown and royal governors made them wary of a strong executive.
choiceExplanations: The treaty did not set terms for state governments.
The colonists' experience with the Crown and royal governors made them wary of a strong executive.
Voters distrusted executives more than legislatures.
The Articles left most powers with the states.
questions.distinguisher: The treaty choice is close because the treaty ended the war, but Americans chose their own state governments.
questions.subskillText: Explain how a historical development or process relates to another historical development or process.

questions.prompt: Under the Articles of Confederation, the national government
choices: consisted of a Congress in which each state had one vote, with no president and no national courts
had a president elected by the people who could veto laws passed by the Congress of the states
had a two-house Congress in which seats were awarded by population and laws passed by majority vote
had a supreme court that could overturn state laws and enforce the treaties that Congress made
questions.explanation: The Articles created a central government with limited power, in which Congress was the only branch and the states kept most authority.
choiceExplanations: The Articles created a central government with limited power, in which Congress was the only branch and the states kept most authority.
The Articles created no president.
Congress had one house with one vote per state.
The Articles created no national court system.
questions.distinguisher: The two-house choice is close because it describes the later Congress, but the Articles created a single house.
questions.subskillText: Identify a historical concept, development, or process.

questions.prompt: Which of the following was a major weakness of the national government under the Articles of Confederation?
choices: Congress controlled the state militias, and the states could not raise troops of their own for defense
The president could dismiss Congress, and no law could pass without his approval in each session
Congress could change the Articles whenever a majority of the states voted in favor of a change
Congress could not tax citizens or regulate trade among the states, and it relied on the states for money
questions.explanation: Without the power to tax or regulate commerce, Congress depended on the states and could not solve the nation's financial and trade problems.
choiceExplanations: The states kept control of their militias.
No president existed under the Articles, so no executive could dismiss Congress.
Amendments required the agreement of all thirteen states.
Without the power to tax or regulate commerce, Congress depended on the states and could not solve the nation's financial and trade problems.
questions.distinguisher: The amendment choice is close because it concerns a weakness in the Articles, but the requirement was unanimity and not a majority.
questions.subskillText: Explain a historical concept, development, or process.

questions.prompt: Shays' Rebellion of 1786–1787 is best described as
choices: a revolt of Loyalists in New York who tried to return the state to British rule after the war
an uprising of indebted farmers in western Massachusetts who closed courts to stop foreclosures
a protest by western Pennsylvania farmers against the federal excise tax on whiskey in 1794
a rebellion of enslaved people in Virginia that led the state to tighten its slave laws
questions.explanation: The rebellion frightened many leaders because the national government could not help the state put it down, and it persuaded many that a stronger government was needed.
choiceExplanations: Shays' Rebellion was a protest of indebted farmers and not a Loyalist revolt.
The rebellion frightened many leaders because the national government could not help the state put it down, and it persuaded many that a stronger government was needed.
This describes the Whiskey Rebellion of 1794.
Shays' Rebellion was in Massachusetts and was not a rebellion of enslaved people.
questions.distinguisher: The Whiskey Rebellion choice is close because both involved farmers, but it took place in the 1790s under the Constitution.
questions.subskillText: Identify a historical concept, development, or process.

questions.prompt: Which of the following best explains why many leaders called for a stronger national government in the 1780s?
choices: Britain had threatened to reconquer the states unless Congress created a national army with a king as commander
The Northwest Ordinance had failed to organize the western lands, and settlers demanded the return of British rule
Difficulties with trade, finances, interstate commerce, foreign relations, and unrest under the Articles
The state legislatures had grown so strong that they asked Congress to abolish all state governments
questions.explanation: The Confederation government struggled with debt, trade, foreign relations, and disorder, and many leaders concluded that it needed more power.
choiceExplanations: Britain did not threaten reconquest on these terms.
The Northwest Ordinance was one of the successes of the Confederation Congress.
The Confederation government struggled with debt, trade, foreign relations, and disorder, and many leaders concluded that it needed more power.
The states did not ask to abolish their own governments.
questions.distinguisher: The Northwest Ordinance choice is close because the ordinance was a Confederation action, but it was a success and not a reason for change.
questions.subskillText: Explain how a historical development or process relates to another historical development or process.

questions.prompt: The Northwest Ordinance of 1787 did which of the following?
choices: Allowed the settlers in the Northwest to decide whether slavery would be legal in each new state
Recognized the land claims of American Indian nations and prohibited any settlement north of the Ohio River
Kept the western lands under the control of the original states, which governed them as colonies
Provided a path to statehood, promoted education and private property, and banned slavery in the territory
questions.explanation: The ordinance set up a process for governing the territory north of the Ohio River and admitting new states, and it set principles for education, property, and slavery.
choiceExplanations: The ordinance banned slavery in the Northwest Territory.
The ordinance did not recognize Native land claims, and settlers moved into the region.
The ordinance provided for admission of new states on equal terms.
The ordinance set up a process for governing the territory north of the Ohio River and admitting new states, and it set principles for education, property, and slavery.
questions.distinguisher: The slavery choice is close because slavery was debated, but the ordinance banned it in the Northwest Territory.
questions.subskillText: Explain a historical concept, development, or process.

questions.prompt: Which of the following was a similarity between most state governments and the national government under the Articles?
choices: Both placed the main power in the legislature and kept the executive weak or nonexistent
Both gave the executive the power to appoint judges and to veto all laws passed by the legislature
Both required every citizen to pay taxes to the national government at rates set by Congress
Both created national courts with the power to overturn the actions of the state governments
questions.explanation: Americans were afraid of strong executives, so both the state constitutions and the Articles placed authority in legislatures.
choiceExplanations: Americans were afraid of strong executives, so both the state constitutions and the Articles placed authority in legislatures.
Both kept executives weak.
Congress could not tax citizens directly.
The Articles created no national courts.
questions.distinguisher: The taxation choice is close because both governments needed money, but under the Articles Congress had to ask the states for it.
questions.subskillText: Identify patterns among or connections between historical developments and processes.

questions.prompt: Which of the following claims about the national government is best supported by the table?
choices: It could tax citizens directly but was unable to raise an army or to conduct foreign relations
It was led by a president who could veto laws and who appointed judges to a national court system
It depended on the states for money and for approval of important decisions
It was able to change its own structure by a majority vote of the members of Congress
questions.explanation: The table shows that Congress could only ask the states for money and that important laws needed nine states, while changes needed all thirteen.
choiceExplanations: The table says Congress could not tax citizens.
The table shows no president and no national courts.
The table shows that Congress could only ask the states for money and that important laws needed nine states, while changes needed all thirteen.
The table says all thirteen states had to approve any change.
questions.distinguisher: The taxation choice is close because it names a power in question, but the table says Congress could not tax citizens.

questions.prompt: Which of the following problems most directly resulted from the feature listed in the table under “Taxes”?
choices: Settlers in the Northwest Territory were allowed to hold enslaved people without any restriction
The national government struggled to pay its war debts and to fund its operations
Britain kept its troops in the forts in the Northwest because the states refused to hold elections
The state governments lost their authority over local matters, including schools and courts
questions.explanation: Because Congress could only ask the states for money, it was often short of funds to pay debts and run the government.
choiceExplanations: The Northwest Ordinance banned slavery, and the ban was not related to taxes.
Because Congress could only ask the states for money, it was often short of funds to pay debts and run the government.
British forts remained for other reasons and not because of state elections.
The states kept their authority under the Articles.
questions.distinguisher: The forts choice is close because it was also a problem under the Articles, but it was not caused by the taxing power.

questions.prompt: The limits on the national government shown in the table are best understood in the context of which of the following?
choices: Americans' fear of concentrated power after their experience with the British Crown and Parliament
The Constitutional Convention's decision to keep the powers of the states and the nation separate
A wish to create a hereditary monarchy that would rule the states after the Treaty of Paris
The need to pay for a large army to defend the western territories against the French in the 1780s
questions.explanation: Having fought against a powerful central authority, many Americans designed a government that would have little power over the states.
choiceExplanations: Having fought against a powerful central authority, many Americans designed a government that would have little power over the states.
The table describes the Articles, which came before the Constitutional Convention.
Americans rejected monarchy.
France had given up its claims to the interior in 1763.
questions.distinguisher: The Convention choice is close because it also concerned the division of power, but the Articles preceded the Convention.
